newsitem.title: UK: Shell move may signal end of Euro-refinery closures.
newsitem.headline: Shell move may signal end of Euro-refinery closures.

text.p: Oil giant Shell's decision to halve capacity at its Berre l'Etang unit France could signal a halt to a swathe of big refinery closures over the last year aimed at cutting overcapacity in Europe.
Alone it will not put much of a dent in lingering overcapacity and is unlikely to fully satisfy shareholders, oil analysts said on Monday.
But the partial closure was a step in the right direction and might prove a shrewd move as oil companies jostled for position in Europe's most overcrowded refining market.

Shell said on Saturday it was seeking formal approval from French authorities to slash crude oil throughput at the Berre refinery in the south of France to 3.5 million tonnes from 6.5 million per year.
This would cut just 60,000 barrels per day (bpd) from European capacity of 12.6 million bpd.

"There will be further optimisation in Europe," said Gundi Royle, oil analyst at Morgan Stanley International in London. But the days of "taking out 100,000 barrels per day in one hit are probably over," she said.
Shell said in December it would sell it's 60,000 bpd Swiss Cressier refinery and close two lubricant plants.

"Confirmation that they are doing something (in southern France) is a relief but it still might not satisfy the market," said Alan Marshall, oil analyst at Robert Fleming Securities in London. "The market was probably expecting a little bit more."
At the root of the problem is a 10 percent excess refining capacity in Europe, particularly evident in the production of gasoline, of which the region exports 14 million tonnes per year.
Restructuring to boost profitability may wane after last year's scheduled closure or sale of five percent of capacity, oil consultants Enerfinance said recently.
Shell's move followed a big shake-up in Europe's downstream sector last year which brought commitments to close or sell nearly 30 million tonnes of capacity or about 600,000 bpd.
European refiners last year also announced closures, mergers or cutbacks at plants in Denmark, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands.

Nick Antill, oil analyst at Barclays De Zoete Wedd, said that France was the most oversupplied market with the lowest downstream margins in Europe. And more importantly southern France was the most competitive area in the country.
Shell's move "will not make very much difference to the group as a whole but it is a perfectly understandable decision," he said.
BP, Shell, Total SA and Exxon Corp, who all have adjacent refineries in southern France, had recently been exploring the possibility of co-ordinated action in the region, analysts said.
But Shell's move means "we might be moving towards independent action" rather than a co-ordinated plan, said Antill.
Other analysts said the spotlight would now move to BP after Total said it would not cut capacity in France.
A BP spokesman said on Monday that the company "was continuing discussions with several interested parties" about the sale of it's Lavera refinery.
"We expect to be in a position to make an announcement by the end of the first quarter," he said.
BP set the ball rolling last year with its January announcement closing the Nerefco section of the Pernis refinery in Rotterdam, a capacity cut of 70,000 bpd.

Kuwait Petroleum's 60,000 bpd Danish refinery and Chevron's 115,000 bpd plant at Pembroke, Britain, also received death sentences last year. Capacity is to be slashed by 60,000 bpd at Exxon's plant in Karlsruhe, Germany.
Analysts say last year's flurry of closures is unlikely to be repeated this year.
"Further restructuring will be slow," said Paris-based Enerfinance in a report.
The French industry ministry said last month it expected refinery investment to fall sharply in France over the next couple of years from 1,853 million francs this year to 1,118 million in 1999.
Shell shares in London were trading down three pence at 1065.5 pence at 1408 GMT on Monday.
